question: What do we call it when cancer cells break away and spread to other parts of the body through the blood or lymph system?
explanation: You've got this! Metastasis is simply the word for when cancer travels from its original spot to start new tumors elsewhere. Great job!

question: How are benign tumors different from malignant ones?

options.A: Benign tumors cannot grow larger than a few millimeters.
options.B: Benign tumors only occur in the blood and lymphatic system.
options.C: Benign tumors do not invade nearby tissues or spread to distant sites.
options.D: Benign tumors consist of dead cells rather than dividing cells.

explanation: Think of benign tumors as staying put in one place without invading surrounding tissues. They aren't cancerous like malignant ones!

question: Which major category of cancer starts in the skin or the lining of internal organs?
explanation: Carcinomas are the most common type of cancer because they begin in the epithelial tissues that line our skin and organs. Keep pushing forward!

question: Which type of cancer starts in the bone marrow and doesn't form solid lumps or tumors?
explanation: Leukemia affects our blood-forming tissues, sending lots of abnormal white blood cells into circulation instead of forming a solid tumor.

question: What is the single biggest cause of cancer worldwide that we can actually prevent?
explanation: Tobacco smoke contains harmful chemicals that damage our DNA. Avoiding tobacco is one of the best health choices anyone can make!

question: Which viral infection is strongly linked to causing cervical cancer in women?
explanation: High-risk strains of Human Papillomavirus (HPV) can cause cellular changes over time, which is why screening and vaccines are so important.

question: What is often one of the very first warning signs of internal cancers like stomach or pancreatic cancer?
explanation: When growing tumors change the body's metabolism and steal nutrients, rapid, unexpected weight loss can happen. Good clinical awareness!

question: A patient shows you a skin mole that has recently changed color and grown irregularly. What should you do first?

options.A: Refer the patient for a prompt medical evaluation and biopsy.
options.B: Advise the patient to monitor the mole at home for another year.
options.C: Apply a medicated topical steroid cream to mole.
options.D: Reassure the patient that changing moles are always benign.

explanation: Any changing mole or spot needs a professional check-up right away to rule out skin cancer. You are learning to protect your patients!

question: What test is always needed to give a 100% definitive diagnosis of cancer?
explanation: Scans and blood tests give us great clues, but looking at a tiny tissue sample under a microscope is what confirms cancer for sure.

question: In the TNM cancer staging system, what does the letter 'M' stand for?
explanation: You've got this! In TNM staging, 'M' tells us if the cancer has traveled or metastasized to other parts of the body.

question: Why do patients on chemotherapy often lose their hair and get mouth sores?

options.A: Chemotherapy drugs target all fast-growing healthy cells along with cancer cells.
options.B: Chemotherapy directly destroys the nervous system.
options.C: Chemotherapy causes severe dehydration in mucosal tissues.
options.D: Chemotherapy blocks the absorption of essential vitamins.

explanation: Chemo attacks rapidly dividing cells—not just cancer cells, but also normal ones like hair roots and mouth linings. That's why these side effects happen!

question: What is the main goal of using radiation therapy in cancer treatment?

options.A: Cleansing the entire circulatory system of loose circulating tumor cells
options.B: Providing systemic relief from widespread metastatic bone pain
options.C: Using targeted high-energy rays to destroy cancer cells in a specific area
options.D: Stimulating the bone marrow to produce extra infection-fighting white blood cells

explanation: Radiation is a localized treatment. It uses powerful beams aimed precisely at the tumor to zap those cancer cells while sparing healthy tissue.

question: A patient on chemotherapy calls the clinic saying their temperature is 38.5°C. What should you tell them to do?

options.A: Drink plenty of cold fluids and monitor the temperature for another day.
options.B: Apply a cool damp cloth to the forehead to bring down the fever.
options.C: Take a dose of paracetamol and rest in bed until tomorrow morning.
options.D: Come to the hospital immediately for a medical evaluation and blood work.

explanation: Fever in a chemo patient is an emergency because their immune system is low. Quick action can save a life!

question: Why should cancer pain medication be given on a regular schedule rather than only when the patient asks?

options.A: It ensures the prescription bottle lasts for the full prescribed month.
options.B: It prevents the patient from developing a physical addiction to the drugs.
options.C: It maintains a steady blood level of medication to prevent severe pain from returning.
options.D: It reduces the risk of experiencing common gastrointestinal side effects.

explanation: Scheduled dosing keeps pain under control before it gets too intense. It's much easier to prevent pain than to chase it once it spikes!

question: When can palliative care start for someone diagnosed with cancer?

options.A: At the time of diagnosis alongside curative treatment
options.B: Only when all chemotherapy and radiation have failed
options.C: Strictly during the final twenty-four hours of life
options.D: Only after the patient is discharged to hospice care

explanation: Palliative care isn't just for the end of life—it can start right away to help manage symptoms and keep the patient comfortable while fighting the disease.

question: What is the primary focus of nursing care for a cancer patient receiving end-of-life support?

options.C: Restoring normal nutritional and metabolic status
options.D: Aggressively treating the underlying tumor growth

explanation: At the end of life, our nursing focus shifts completely to surrounding the patient and family with comfort, peace, and dignity.
